citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: A radius-$r$ Euclidean ball has finite $r2^{-k}$-nets $T_k$ with $|T_k|\le(C_d2^k)^d$ for a finite dimension-dependent constant $C_d$: cover a containing cube by a grid of side at most $r2^{-k}/\sqrt d$ and retain one point from each grid cell meeting the ball. The union of these nets is countable and dense. For each fixed sample in the common full set, $t\mapsto f_t(X_i)$ is Lipschitz and hence continuous, so the supremum over the ball equals the supremum over that countable union and is measurable. The same grid argument on the compact pair domain makes the pairwise-modulus supremum measurable. The first supremum is integrable because $|f_t|\le rM$ and $PM<\infty$.

Conditional on $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $R_n(t)=n^{-1/2}\sum_i\varepsilon_i f_t(X_i)$, with signs on the product probability space [F2]. Since $E e^{\lambda\varepsilon a}=\cosh(\lambda a)\le e^{\lambda^2a^2/2}$, its increments satisfy $E_\varepsilon e^{\lambda(R_n(t)-R_n(s))}\le e^{\lambda^2(P_nM^2)\|t-s\|_2^2/2}$. The inequality for $\cosh$ follows by integrating $(\log\cosh u)'=\tanh u\le u$ for $u\ge0$ and using evenness. Thus each increment is sub-Gaussian with scale $(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\|t-s\|_2$.

By [F1] and [F2], adjoin an independent IID copy $X'_1,\ldots,X'_n$ and independent signs $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, each equally likely. For each fixed original sample, the supremum of absolute values of affine functions of the ghost sample is convex; Jensen's inequality therefore bounds $E\sup_t|\sqrt n(P_n-P)f_t|$ by $E\sup_t|n^{-1/2}\sum_i(f_t(X_i)-f_t(X'_i))|$. Each pair $(X_i,X'_i)$ is exchangeable, so independently swapping the members of each pair with sign $\varepsilon_i$ preserves the joint law. The triangle inequality then bounds the last expectation by $2E E_\varepsilon\sup_t|n^{-1/2}\sum_i\varepsilon_i f_t(X_i)|$.

Set $T_0=\{0\}$ and fix an ordering of each finite net $T_k$. For each $k\ge1$, let $\pi_k(t)$ be the first nearest point in that ordering; then $\|\pi_k(t)-\pi_{k-1}(t)\|_2\le 3r2^{-k}$. For $N$ centered sub-Gaussian variables of scale at most $\sigma$, the exponential-moment bound gives $E\max_{j\le N}|Y_j|\le \log(2N)/\lambda+\lambda\sigma^2/2$ for every $\lambda>0$; minimizing at $\lambda=\sqrt{2\log(2N)}/\sigma$ gives $\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2N)}$. Apply this to the at most $|T_k||T_{k-1}|$ links and sum the resulting bounds: $E_\varepsilon\sup_t|R_n(t)|\le C_d r(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}\sqrt{k}\le C'_d r(P_nM^2)^{1/2}$. Continuity of the sample paths passes from the nets to the full ball.

Combine the symmetrization bound in step 2.1 with step 2.2 and use $E(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\le(PM^2)^{1/2}$, which is Cauchy--Schwarz. Absorbing the numerical factors into $C_d$ proves the first expectation inequality.

For the modulus bound, apply the ghost-sample and independent-swap argument of step 2.1 to the class $g_{s,t}=f_t-f_s$ indexed by the compact set $D_{r,\varepsilon}=\{(s,t):\|s\|_2,\|t\|_2\le r,\ \|t-s\|_2\le\varepsilon\}$. Conditional on the data, its signed process is $U_n(s,t)=R_n(t)-R_n(s)$; its increments between $(s,t)$ and $(s',t')$ are sub-Gaussian with scale at most $(P_nM^2)^{1/2}(\|s-s'\|_2+\|t-t'\|_2)$ by step 1.2. At pair-mesh $\varepsilon2^{-k}$, grid the ambient product ball, retain one point from each cell meeting $D_{r,\varepsilon}$, and adjoin $(0,0)$. The resulting finite nets have at most $(C r2^k/\varepsilon)^{2d}$ points after increasing the dimension-dependent $C$. The maximum on the initial net has conditional expectation at most $(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\varepsilon\sqrt{2\log(2N_0)}$, since every pair in $D_{r,\varepsilon}$ has $\|t-s\|_2\le\varepsilon$ and $U_n(0,0)=0$. Between consecutive nets, the link lengths are at most a constant times $\varepsilon2^{-k}$ and the number of links is at most $N_kN_{k-1}$. The sub-Gaussian maximum bound from step 2.2 therefore bounds the expected maximum link at level $k$ by $C_d(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\varepsilon2^{-k}\sqrt{\log(e r/\varepsilon)+k}$. Summing over $k\ge1$ gives $C_d(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(e r/\varepsilon)}$; continuity extends the net bound to $D_{r,\varepsilon}$. Symmetrization and $E(P_nM^2)^{1/2}\le(PM^2)^{1/2}$ prove the second inequality, after increasing $C_d$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $Q_n$ be the posterior law of $H_n$. The contraction premise implies that $(Q_n)$ is tight in probability: for every $\eta,\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $R$ such that $\limsup_nP_{0,n}\{Q_n(\|h\|_2>R)>\eta\}<\varepsilon$. Otherwise there would be $\eta,\varepsilon>0$ and increasing radii $R_k\to\infty$ with indices $n_k$ for which $P_{0,n_k}\{Q_{n_k}(\|h\|_2>R_k)>\eta\}>\varepsilon$. Define $M_n=R_k$ for $n_k\le n<n_{k+1}$, with any positive initial values. Then $M_n\to\infty$ and the assumed contraction fails along $n_k$, a contradiction.

The supplied common-dominator density setup [F1, F2] makes the posterior likelihood ratio well-defined on the stated $P_{0,n}$-full set. Fix $R>0$ and put $K_R=\{h:\|h\|_2\le R\}$. Since $\theta^*$ is interior and $\delta_n\to0$, $\theta^*+\delta_nK_R\subset\Theta$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Relative to Lebesgue measure on $K_R$, the unnormalized posterior density for $H_n$ is proportional to $q_n(h)=\exp(\ell_n(\theta^*+\delta_nh))\pi(\theta^*+\delta_nh)$; the Jacobian $\delta_n^d$ cancels on conditioning on $K_R$. Set $g_n(h)=\exp(h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TVh)$. By compact-uniform LAN and continuity of $\pi$ at $\theta^*$, $q_n(h)/g_n(h)=\pi(\theta^*)(1+o_{P_{0,n}}(1))$ uniformly on $K_R$. Completing the square gives $g_n$ proportional to the density in [F5] with mean $V^{-1}\Delta_n$ and covariance $V^{-1}$. If $w_n=q_n/g_n$ and $\bar w_n=\int_{K_R}w_n\,dG_n^{K_R}$, where $G_n^{K_R}$ is the Gaussian law conditioned on $K_R$, the two conditional densities have ratio $w_n/\bar w_n$. Uniform convergence $w_n/\pi(\theta^*)\to1$ implies $\bar w_n/\pi(\theta^*)\to1$, so $\sup_{K_R}|w_n/\bar w_n-1|=o_{P_{0,n}}(1)$ and their total-variation distance tends to zero.

By [F6] and the assumed $\Delta_n=O_{P_{0,n}}(1)$, the Gaussian means $V^{-1}\Delta_n$ are bounded in probability. For any fixed bound on the mean, its Gaussian probability outside $K_R$ is at most the centered $N_d(0,V^{-1})$ probability outside a ball whose radius tends to infinity with $R$. That centered probability tends to zero because the decreasing complements of the balls have empty intersection and the law is a probability. Thus the Gaussian tails are tight in probability as $R\to\infty$.

For any two probability measures $P,Q$ and measurable $K$, their restrictions conditioned on $K$ satisfy $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le \|P(\cdot\mid K)-Q(\cdot\mid K)\|_{\rm TV}+2P(K^c)+2Q(K^c)$ whenever both conditioning probabilities are positive. Indeed, for any event $A$, split it into $A\cap K$ and $A\cap K^c$, compare the two conditional masses on $K$, and use $|P(K)-Q(K)|\le P(K^c)+Q(K^c)$. Choose $R$ so the posterior tail from step 1.1 and Gaussian tail from step 1.3 are arbitrarily small in probability; the conditional distance tends to zero for this fixed $R$ by step 1.2. Letting the tail tolerance decrease to zero proves the asserted full total-variation convergence under [F3].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[def-qmd-path]]. Write $p_0=p_{\theta_0}$,
$p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, and $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Let
$$\alpha(u):=P_{\theta_0+u}(p_0=0),\qquad \beta(u):=P_0(p_u=0).$$
Then $\alpha(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ and $\beta(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ as $u\to0$.

Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $X^{(n)}$ have law $P_{0,n}$ on a measurable
space, and let $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, $d\ge1$. Suppose a
supplied sigma-finite measure $\mu_n$ dominates $P_{0,n}$ and the model laws
$P_{n,\theta}$, and suppose jointly measurable finite-valued densities
$p_{0,n}$ and $p_{n,\theta}$ are supplied. Fix an interior point
$\theta^*\in\Theta$ with $p_{n,\theta^*}(X^{(n)})>0$
$P_{0,n}$-almost surely. Let the prior be a proper Lebesgue density $\pi$
continuous and strictly positive on a neighbourhood of $\theta^*$, and assume
the displayed likelihood integral is finite and positive almost surely so it
defines the posterior
$$\Pi_n(A\mid X^{(n)})=\frac{\int_Ap_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{\int_\Theta p_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}.$$
For $\delta_n>0$ with $\delta_n\to0$, write
$$\ell_n(\theta)=\log\frac{p_{n,\theta}(X^{(n)})}{p_{n,\theta^*}(X^{(n)})}.$$
Assume $V$ is a fixed symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix,
$\Delta_n=O_{P_{0,n}}(1)$, and for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{h\in K}\left|\ell_n(\theta^*+\delta_nh)-h^T\Delta_n+\tfrac12h^TVh\right|=o_{P_{0,n}}(1).$$
Also assume that for every deterministic sequence $M_n\to\infty$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left(\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2>\delta_nM_n\mid X^{(n)}\right)=o_{P_{0,n}}(1).$$
Then the posterior law of $H_n=\delta_n^{-1}(\theta-\theta^*)$ satisfies
$$\left\|\Pi_n(H_n\in\cdot\mid X^{(n)})-N_d(V^{-1}\Delta_n,V^{-1})\right\|_{\rm TV}=o_{P_{0,n}}(1),$$
where $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable sets. The
LAN condition concerns likelihood-density ratios on the $P_{0,n}$-full set
where the denominator is positive; it does not assert a Radon–Nikodym
derivative for the entire local model law.

derivations.claim: By [A1, F1, F2], $\alpha(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ and $\beta(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$. For fixed compact $H$ with $\|h\|_2\le R$, this little-$o$ relation is uniform over $\|u\|_2\le R/\sqrt n$: $n\sup_{h\in H}\alpha(h/\sqrt n)\to0$ and $n\sup_{h\in H}\beta(h/\sqrt n)\to0$.

Under $P_0$, each observation lies in $S$ almost surely. On $S$, the actual density ratio is $p_{\theta^*+u}/p_0=(1-\alpha(u))q_u$. For $\alpha\le1/2$, $|\log(1-\alpha)|\le2\alpha$, so step 1.1 gives $\sup_{h\in H}\left|n\log(1-\alpha(h/\sqrt n))\right|\le2n\sup_{h\in H}\alpha(h/\sqrt n)\longrightarrow0.$ Thus the actual posterior likelihood ratios have the same compact-uniform LAN expansion as the normalized proxy. The zero-overlap bound in step 1.1 is recorded separately; compact-uniform positivity is supplied by the proxy-LAN hypothesis, not inferred from pointwise QMD.

For each local $u$, write $P_{\theta^*+u}=(1-\alpha(u))\bar P_u+\alpha(u)S_u$, where $\bar P_u=q_uP_0$ is supported on $S$ and $S_u$ is the normalized restriction to $S^c$ when $\alpha(u)>0$. In the product mixture, the all-$\bar P_u$ component has weight $(1-\alpha(u))^n$ and every other component is supported outside $S^n$. Hence $\|P_{\theta^*+u}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_u^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}=1-(1-\alpha(u))^n\le n\alpha(u).$ Step 1.1 makes this $o(1)$ uniformly for $h\in H$. This comparison is between probability laws and does not identify a full Radon–Nikodym derivative for $P_{\theta^*+u}^{\otimes n}$.

Step 2.1 supplies the compact-uniform LAN premise for the actual posterior likelihood ratios; the prior, evidence, and posterior-rate hypotheses are those of [F5]. Applying [F5] with $\delta_n=n^{-1/2}$ proves the BvM limit. The fixed-sequence assertion [F4] alone would not justify the compact supremum used here.

$\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, $d\ge1$. Suppose a sigma-finite measure
$\mu$ and jointly measurable finite-valued densities $p_0,p_\theta$ are
supplied, with $P_0(dx)=p_0(x)\mu(dx)$, $P_\theta(dx)=p_\theta(x)\mu(dx)$,
and $p_{\theta^*}>0$ $P_0$-almost surely. Define the directional contrast
$$K(\theta)=E_0\log\frac{p_0(X)}{p_\theta(X)}.$$
Assume $K$ is finite near an interior point $\theta^*$, $\theta^*$ is a
finite minimizer of $K$, and, for $t\to0$,
$$E_0\log\frac{p_{\theta^*}(X)}{p_{\theta^*+t}(X)}=\tfrac12t^TVt+o(\|t\|_2^2)$$
for a fixed symmetric positive-definite matrix $V$. Assume also that a
measurable random vector $s(X)\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfies
$$\frac{\log p_{\theta^*+t}(X)-\log p_{\theta^*}(X)-t^Ts(X)}{\|t\|_2}\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0$-probability as $t\to0$ through nonzero vectors, and that on a
neighbourhood $U$ of $\theta^*$ there is a common $P_0$-almost-sure bound
$$\left|\log\frac{p_{\theta_1}(X)}{p_{\theta_2}(X)}\right|\le M(X)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|_2\qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in U),$$

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The log-Lipschitz envelope and [F3] give $E_0\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|G_nf_t|\le C r$ for $r\le\rho$, where $G_n=\sqrt n(P_n-P_0)$ and $C=C_d(E_0M^2)^{1/2}$.

Let $\eta_n=n(\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}P_n\log p_\theta-P_n\log p_{\widehat\theta_n})$. The assumption gives $\eta_n=o_{P_0}(1)$ by [F2]. For fixed $A\ge1$, set $r_j=2^jA/\sqrt n$ and consider shells $r_j\le\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*\|_2\le2r_j$ with $2r_j\le\rho$. On such a shell, approximate maximization implies $nP_nf_{\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*}\ge-\eta_n$, while step 1.1 bounds the mean term above by $-cnr_j^2$. On $\{\eta_n\le cA^2/2\}$ this forces $\sup_{\|t\|\le2r_j}|G_nf_t|\ge(c/2)\sqrt n r_j^2$. Markov's inequality and step 1.1 bound the shell probability by $C'/(\sqrt n r_j)=C'/(2^jA)$. Summing over the shells, using consistency to remove $\|\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*\|>\rho/4$, and then taking $A\to\infty$ proves $\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*)=O_{P_0}(1)$.

Set $\widehat h_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta^*)$ and $h_n^*=V^{-1}S_n$. By [F4] the score sums converge in distribution; [F5] makes $S_n$ and $h_n^*$ bounded in probability. Step 2.1 gives the same for $\widehat h_n$. Since $\theta^*$ is interior, $\theta^*+h_n^*/\sqrt n\in\Theta$ with probability tending to one.

On any fixed ball containing $\widehat h_n$ and $h_n^*$ with probability arbitrarily close to one, [F1] expands both log likelihoods uniformly. Approximate maximization then gives $Q_n(\widehat h_n)\ge Q_n(h_n^*)-o_{P_0}(1),\qquad Q_n(h)=h^TS_n-\tfrac12h^TVh.$ Completing the square gives $Q_n(h_n^*)-Q_n(\widehat h_n)=\tfrac12(\widehat h_n-h_n^*)^TV(\widehat h_n-h_n^*)\ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(V)\|\widehat h_n-h_n^*\|_2^2$. Hence $\widehat h_n-h_n^*=o_{P_0}(1)$.
